rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city they fled was Ephesus, and the youths woke from their long sleep hungry, so they asked for food.
rows.anchor: ذلك الذي يحدث به يمليخا نفسه فيما أخبر أصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Yamlīkha returned with the old coin, two city officials suspected he had found a treasure; he said it was his fathers’ currency and could not explain his situation.
rows.anchor: هذا الورق يشهد عليك أنك قد وجدت كنزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one recognized Yamlīkha or his father; some called him mad, while the officials accused him of lying and threatened torture until he confessed.
rows.anchor: ولا أباه، فقال له أحدهما: أنت رجل كذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked about Daqyanus, the townspeople said no such man lived and that the king had died long ago; Yamlīkha realized centuries had passed.
rows.anchor: ليس على وجه الأرض رجل اسمه دقينوس، ولم يكن إلا ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yamlīkha said he had seen Daqyanus enter Ephesus the previous evening, asked the officials to see his companions, and Areus recognized a possible sign from God.
rows.anchor: يا قوم لعل هذه آية من آيات الله جعلها لكم على يدي هذا الفتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Areus, Astius, and the townspeople, both prominent and ordinary, accompanied Yamlīkha toward the cave to see the sleepers.
rows.anchor: فانطلق معه أريوس وأسطيوس، وانطلق معهم أهل المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Yamlīkha delayed, his companions feared Daqyanus had captured him; hearing horses, they prayed, exchanged farewells, and expected to face the tyrant.
rows.anchor: ظنوا أنه قد أخذ فذهب به إلى ملكهم دقينوس الذي هربوا منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They found Areus and the townspeople at the cave instead; Yamlīkha told the youths what happened, and they understood God had awakened them as a sign of resurrection.
rows.anchor: فعرفوا عند ذلك أنهم كانوا نياما بأمر الله ذلك الزمان كله، وإنما أوقظوا ليكونوا آية للناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sealed copper chest held lead tablets naming the youths and saying they fled Daqyanus to protect their faith; the king had sealed their cave with stones.
rows.anchor: مخافة أن يفتنهم عن دينهم، فدخلوا هذا الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After reading the tablets, the townspeople praised God for showing them a sign of resurrection and found the youths alive-looking, unchanged, and seated in the cave.
rows.anchor: فوجدوا فيه لوحين من رصاص، مكتوبا فيهما كتاب، فقرأهما فوجد فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous king Theodosius came, embraced and wept over the youths, who welcomed him and then returned to their resting places and died.
rows.anchor: فلما رأى الفتية تيذوسيس، فرحوا به، وخروا سجودا على وجوههم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king first ordered gold coffins, but after the youths asked in a dream to remain on earth, he placed them in teak; fear then barred entry, and their cave became a mosque and annual festival site.
rows.anchor: فاتركنا كما كنا في الكهف على التراب حتى يبعثنا الله منه، فأمر الملك حينئذ بتابوت من ساج

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: The youths were raised under a Muslim king, hungry; one judged they had slept a day or less, then deferred the true duration to God and went to buy food with old coins.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير، قال: بعثهم الله يعني الفتية أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: The old coins dated from a king three hundred and nine years earlier; the merchant took Yamlīkha to the Muslim king, and the account matched an archived tablet.
rows.anchor: هذه الورق من ضرب فلان بن فلان منذ ثلاثمائة وتسع سنين أنت أصبت كنزا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Pagans claimed the youths as their ancestors and proposed a building for worship; Muslims claimed them as fellow believers and proposed a mosque for prayer.
rows.anchor: فقال المشركون: نحن أحق بهم هؤلاء أبناء آبائنا، وقال المسلمون: نحن أحق بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God raised the youths so they would question one another, then exposed them to doubters as proof that He can raise the dead, as the verse itself explains.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى بعثهم من رقدتهم ليتساءلوا بينهم كما بينا قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinan and some Iraqi readers pronounce ورقكم with fatḥa on wāw and kasra on rāʾ; most Kufan and Basran readers make rāʾ quiescent.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ذلك عامة قراء أهل المدينة وبعض العراقيين {بورقكم هذه} [الكهف: 19] بفتح الواو وكسر الراء والقاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Meccan readers kasrate rāʾ and assimilate qāf into kāf; all readings carry the same meaning and reflect known Arabic forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأه بعض المكيين بكسر الراء، وإدغام القاف في الكاف، وكل هذه القراءات متفقات المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The original form is ورق with wāw fatḥa and rāʾ and qāf kasra, so al-Ṭabarī prefers that reading while accepting the others as sound forms of Arabic.
rows.anchor: غير أن الأصل في ذلك فتح الواو وكسر الراء والقاف

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: A report transmitted from Muqātil identifies the youth sent with the coins as Yamlīkh.
rows.anchor: عن مقاتل، {فابعثوا أحدكم بورقكم هذه} [الكهف: 19] اسمه يمليخ

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima interprets أزكى طعاما as asking which resident has the most food.
rows.anchor: عن أبي حصين، عن عكرمة، {أيها أزكى طعاما} [الكهف: 19] قال: أكثر

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr interprets أزكى طعاما as asking which food is more lawful.
rows.anchor: عن أبي حصين، عن سعيد بن جبير: {أيها أزكى طعاما} [الكهف: 19] قال: أحل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda gives the sense as asking which food is better.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، في قوله: {أزكى طعاما} [الكهف: 19] قال: خير طعاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers lawful and pure food: requiring the best makes sense whether a seller has much or little, and lawful good food outweighs abundant unlawful food.
rows.anchor: وأولى الأقوال عندي في ذلك بالصواب: قول من قال: معنى ذلك: أحل وأطهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The more-food interpretation draws on Arabic usage where zakā can mean increase; an unnamed poem uses أزكى to mean more, but al-Ṭabarī says that does not decide the verse’s sense.
rows.anchor: وللسبع أزكى من ثلاث وأطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أيها is grammatically attached to the city but means its inhabitants, since listeners understand that the food belongs to people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: {فلينظر أيها} [الكهف: 19] فأضيف إلى كناية المدينة، والمراد بها أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths may have meant which food was lawful because they had left an idolatrous people and would not permit themselves to eat their sacrificial meat.
rows.anchor: من أجل أنهم كانوا فارقوا قومهم وهم أهل أوثان

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: رزق means food or sustenance to eat.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير، {فليأتكم برزق منه} [الكهف: 19] قال: بطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger should act gently and cautiously while shopping, traveling, and entering the city, and ensure no one learns about the youths.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {وليتلطف} [الكهف: 19] يقول: وليترفق في شرائه ما يشتري، وفي طريقه ودخوله المدينة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj explains يرجموكم as verbally insulting and hurting the youths if Daqyanus and his followers discover them.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج، في قوله: {إنهم إن يظهروا عليكم يرجموكم} [الكهف: 20] قال: يشتموكم بالقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God revived the youths in their former appearance so they could question one another, He disclosed them to doubters so they would recognize His power to raise the dead and the certainty of the Hour.
rows.anchor: كذلك أطلعنا عليهم الفريق الآخر الذين كانوا في شك من قدرة الله على إحياء الموتى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God revealed the youths to those who denied the account, so they would know the promise and the Hour are real.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {وكذلك أعثرنا عليهم} [الكهف: 21] يقول: أطلعنا عليهم ليعلم من كذب بهذا الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disputants were Theodosius’s people debating whether God recreates His servants after death and decay.
rows.anchor: مماته، أمنشئهم هو أم غير منشئهم؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those finding the sleepers proposed building over them, saying their Lord knew their circumstances; the people who prevailed then resolved to make a mosque there.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {قال الذين غلبوا على أمرهم} [الكهف: 21] يقول جل ثناؤه: قال القوم الذين غلبوا على أمر أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies those who prevailed and proposed the mosque as the youths’ enemies.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قوله: {قال الذين غلبوا على أمرهم لنتخذن عليهم مسجدا} [الكهف: 21] قال: يعني عدوهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr’s account distinguishes pagans who wanted a building and worship from Muslims who wanted a mosque for prayer.
rows.anchor: فقال المشركون: نبني عليهم بنيانا، فإنهم أبناء آبائنا، ونعبد الله فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God instructed the Prophet not to assert that a future event will certainly happen without connecting it to God’s will, because nothing occurs apart from His will.
rows.anchor: من الأمور أنه كائن لا محالة، إلا أن يصله بمشيئة الله، لأنه لا يكون شيء إلا بمشيئة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction followed the Prophet’s promise to answer three questions the next day without saying إن شاء الله; revelation was delayed fifteen days, distressing him, before the answers came.
rows.anchor: وعد سائليه عن المسائل الثلاث اللواتي قد ذكرناها فيما مضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended exception is to say إن شاء الله; the phrase about what God wills is elliptical for saying that, with the omitted verb understood from context.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الكلام: إلا أن تقول معه: إن شاء الله، فترك ذكر تقول اكتفاء بما ذكر منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative grammarian takes the exception to qualify the utterance itself, but al-Ṭabarī calls this distant from the apparent sense and contrary to transmitted exegesis.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه بعيد من المفهوم بالظاهر من التنزيل مع خلافه تأويل أهل التأويل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās via Mujāhid says someone who forgot an oath’s exception may still add it, even as late as a year.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية، في قوله

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says that when one remembers the omitted exception, one should then say it.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية، في قوله {ولا تقولن لشيء إني فاعل ذلك غدا إلا أن يشاء الله واذكر ربك إذا نسيت} [الكهف: 24] الاستثناء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A report attributed to al-Ḥasan says that when one remembers not saying God willing, one should say it then.
rows.anchor: بلغني أن الحسن، قال: إذا ذكر أنه لم يقل: إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima offers another interpretation: remember your Lord when you disobey.
rows.anchor: عن ثابت، عن عكرمة، في قول الله: {واذكر ربك إذا نسيت} [الكهف: 24] قال: اذكر ربك إذا عصيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers remember your Lord when you have left off remembering Him, since nisyān in Arabic can mean leaving something.
rows.anchor: وأولى القولين في ذلك بالصواب، قول من قال: معناه: واذكر ربك إذا تركت ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One may add the exception even after breaking the oath to remove the sin of omission, but the expiation remains due unless the exception was joined to the original oath.
rows.anchor: فأما الكفارة فلا تسقط عنه بحال، إلا أن يكون استثناؤه موصولا بيمينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports allowing an exception after a year, a month, or the same sitting all address relief from blame after delay; none says that delayed exception erases an expiation for breaking the oath.
rows.anchor: ولو بعد عشر سنين، وأنه باستثنائه وقيله إن شاء الله بعد حين من حال حلفه، يسقط عنه الحرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should say that perhaps God will guide him to something more rightly guided than the future statement he promised, if God wills it.
rows.anchor: ولعل الله أن يهديني فيسددني لأسد مما وعدتكم وأخبرتكم أنه سيكون

rows.speaker: محمد رجل من أهل الكوفة
rows.claim: A Kufa Qurʾān interpreter says that if someone forgets to say God willing, saying the prayer for nearer guidance serves as repentance or expiation for that omission.
rows.anchor: عن أبيه، عن محمد رجل من أهل الكوفة كان يفسر القرآن، وكان يجلس إليه يحيى بن عباد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the statement that the youths stayed three hundred years and nine more is what the People of the Book say, and God corrects them in the next verse.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {ولبثوا في كهفهم ثلاث مائة سنين وازدادوا تسعا} [الكهف: 25] هذا قول أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: مطر الوراق
rows.claim: Maṭar al-Warrāq likewise says the duration was something Jews said, which God refuted by saying He knows best how long they remained.
rows.anchor: عن مطر الوراق، في قول الله: {ولبثوا في كهفهم ثلاث مائة سنين} [الكهف: 25] قال: إنما هو شيء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid takes the three hundred years and nine more as the number of years they actually remained.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، ولبثوا في كهفهم ثلاث مائة سنين

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr explicitly glosses the added nine as nine years.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير، قال: {ولبثوا في كهفهم ثلاث مائة سنين وازدادوا تسعا} [الكهف: 25] قال: وتسع سنين

rows.speaker: الضحاك بن مزاحم
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says that after the verse first stated three hundred, people asked whether this meant days, months, or years, and the clarification came that it was years plus nine.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك بن مزاحم، قال: نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses their cave as lying between two mountains.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، ولبثوا في كهفهم قال: بين جبلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī holds that God states their actual stay: three hundred years and nine from entering the cave until He awakened and exposed them; the verse gives this directly.
rows.anchor: وأولى الأقوال في ذلك بالصواب أن يقال كما قال الله عز ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects treating 18:25 as an unmarked quotation of the People of the Book: the text gives no signal of reported speech, and a claim about God’s words needs proof.
rows.anchor: ولم يضع دليلا على أن ذلك خبر منه عن قول قوم قالوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads God knows best how long they remained as referring to the time after their souls were taken following their awakening, up to the revelation; only God or one informed by Him knows it.
rows.anchor: الله أعلم بما لبثوا بعد أن قبض أرواحهم، من بعد أن بعثهم من رقدتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinan, Basran, and some Kufan readers add tanwīn to three hundred and read the following word as an explanation; most Kufans construct the number directly with سنين.
rows.anchor: فقرأت ذلك عامة قراء المدينة والبصرة وبعض الكوفيين {ثلاث مائة سنين} [الكهف: 25] بتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers tanwīn because hundreds are normally explained by a singular noun; plural explanations occur, but less often.
rows.anchor: وأولى القراءتين في ذلك عندي بالصواب قراءة من قرأه: {ثلاث مائة} [الكهف: 25] بالتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the unseen of heaven and earth without anything escaping or being hidden from Him, so people should leave to Him the unknown duration after the youths’ awakening.
rows.anchor: الله الواحد القهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أبصر به وأسمع is emphatic praise: God sees every existing thing and hears every sound, with nothing hidden from His sight or hearing.
rows.anchor: فلا أحد أبصر من الله ولا أسمع، تبارك وتعالى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says no one sees or hears better than God.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، {أبصر به وأسمع} [الكهف: 26] فلا أحد أبصر من الله ولا أسمع

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God sees people’s deeds and hears them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قوله: {أبصر به وأسمع ما لهم من دونه من ولي} [الكهف: 26] قال: يرى أعمالهم، ويسمع ذلك منهم سميعا بصيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creatures have no protector apart from their Lord to manage their affairs; God alone decides and governs them, without a partner in judgment.
rows.anchor: وتدبيرهم وتصريفهم فيما شاء وأحب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to recite and follow the revealed Book, obeying its commands and prohibitions and practicing its lawful and forbidden rulings, or face the consequence of disobedience.
rows.anchor: فتكون من الهالكين، وذلك أن مصير من خالفه، وترك اتباعه يوم القيامة إلى جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can alter God’s announced words of threat against sinners who oppose the revealed Book.
rows.anchor: لا مغير لما أوعد بكلماته التي أنزلها عليك أهل معاصيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ملتحدا means a place of refuge or escape; the Prophet could find nowhere to turn from God’s warning because divine power encompasses all creation.
rows.anchor: أحد منهم على الهرب من أمر أراد به

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses ملتحدا as a refuge.
rows.anchor: عن منصور، عن مجاهد، في قوله: {ملتحدا} [الكهف: 27] قال: ملجأ

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses ملتحدا as a refuge or place of recourse.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، {ولن تجد من دونه ملتحدا} [الكهف: 27] قال: موئلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word is an iftiʿāl form from laḥd, turning toward a side; laḥd names the side niche of a grave, and ilḥād in religion means turning away from it.
rows.anchor: يقال منه: لحدت إلى كذا: إذا ملت إليه، ومنه قيل للحد: لحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to remain with companions who remember God through praise, glorification, prayer, and other good works, seeking God’s face rather than worldly gain.
rows.anchor: بذكرهم إياه بالتسبيح والتحميد والتهليل والدعاء والأعمال الصالحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard readers recite بالغداة; ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī are reported to read بالغدوة.
rows.anchor: عامر وأبي عبد الرحمن السلمي أنهما كانا يقرآنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabists disfavor بالغدوة because غدوة is already definite, takes no alif-lām or genitive construction; al-Ṭabarī follows the readers’ consensus on بالغداة.
rows.anchor: والقراءة عندنا في ذلك ما عليه القراء في الأمصار لا نستجيز غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ولا تعد عيناك means do not turn your gaze from the believers to others; the expression derives from surpassing or going beyond something.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج، قال: قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the command as not passing over the believers for other people.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج، قال: قال ابن عباس، في قوله: {ولا تعد عيناك عنهم} [الكهف: 28] قال: لا تجاوزهم إلى غيرهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says some people asked the Prophet to leave the humble believers and sit with Arab nobles; the verse forbade neglecting or despising the believers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قوله

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن سهل بن حنيف
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sahl reports that after the verse came, the Prophet found poorly dressed people remembering God, sat with them, and praised God for ordering his patience with them.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الرحمن بن سهل بن حنيف، أن هذه الآية، لما نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly adornment sought was status from keeping company with prominent polytheist leaders who objected to the Prophet’s poor companions.
rows.anchor: يريد زينة الحياة الدنيا: مجالسة أولئك العظماء الأشراف

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: A report from Khabbāb’s story says the Prophet was seen with Khabbāb, Ṣuhayb, and Bilāl; visitors asked him to make the poor men leave when they arrived.
rows.anchor: عن خباب، في قصة ذكرها عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عيينة بن حصن
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn, before becoming Muslim, complained of Salmān’s smell and requested a separate gathering.
rows.anchor: أخبرت أن عيينة بن حصن قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قبل أن يسلم: لقد آذاني ريح سلمان الفارسي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the Prophet praised God for placing in his community people with whom he was commanded to remain patient.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قال: ذكر لنا أنه لما نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explains زينة الحياة الدنيا here as the worldly elite.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قوله {تريد زينة الحياة الدنيا} [الكهف: 28] قال: تريد أشراف الدنيا

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: Salmān reports that Uyayna, al-Aqraʿ, and their delegation wanted the Prophet to remove poor believers in wool garments so they could sit with him and learn; he found the believers remembering God and said their life and death were with him.
rows.anchor: عن سلمان الفارسي، قال: جاءت المؤلفة قلوبهم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people whose hearts God left heedless were the unbelieving leaders who asked that the worshippers be expelled; they chose desire over obedience.
rows.anchor: اتباع أمر الله ونهيه، وآثر هوى نفسه على طاعة ربه، وهم فيما ذكر: عيينة بن حصن

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: Khabbāb’s report identifies the leaders who sought the separation as ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الكنود، عن خباب، {ولا تطع من أغفلنا قلبه عن ذكرنا} [الكهف: 28] قال: عيينة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses فرطا as waste or loss.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، في قول الله: {وكان أمره فرطا} [الكهف: 28] قال ابن عمرو في حديثه قال: ضائعا

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: Dāwūd interprets فرطا as remorse.
rows.anchor: عن داود، {فرطا} [الكهف: 28] قال: ندامة

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: Khabbāb’s report through al-Suddī interprets فرطا as destruction.
rows.anchor: عن خباب، {وكان أمره فرطا} [الكهف: 28] قال: هلاكا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets فرطا as being opposed to the truth.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: {وكان أمره فرطا} [الكهف: 28] قال: مخالفا للحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers waste and destruction: the careless person exceeds bounds through vanity, pride, and contempt for believers, thereby losing the truth and perishing.
rows.anchor: وكان أمر هذا الذي أغفلنا قلبه عن ذكرنا في الرياء والكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked how ʿĀṣim read the phrase, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh gives كان أمره فرطا; al-Ṭabarī adds that ʿUyayna used to boast, saying I, I.
rows.anchor: كيف قرأ عاصم؟ فقال {كان أمره فرطا} [الكهف: 28] قال أبو كريب: قال أبو بكر: كان عيينة بن حصن يفخر بقول أنا وأنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth comes from God; guidance and misguidance are in His hand, while the Prophet is not to dismiss believers to satisfy the elite.
rows.anchor: يهدي من يشاء منكم للرشاد، فيؤمن، ويضل من يشاء عن الهدى فيكفر، ليس إلي من ذلك شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says whom God wills to believe believes and whom He wills to disbelieve disbelieves, consistent with the statement that human willing depends on God’s will.
rows.anchor: عن علي، عن ابن عباس، قوله: {فمن شاء فليؤمن ومن شاء فليكفر} [الكهف: 29] يقول: من شاء الله له الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever wishes may believe or disbelieve is a threat and warning, not permission to choose unbelief; the following threat of fire establishes this.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا بإطلاق من الله الكفر لمن شاء، والإيمان لمن أراد، وإنما هو تهديد ووعيد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid likewise calls the statement a divine threat that cannot be evaded.
rows.anchor: عن عمر بن حبيب، عن داود، عن مجاهد،

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd links this threat to 41:40 and says such language is neither appeasement nor a delegation of choice.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أعتدنا means prepared, from the word for provision or readiness; the wrongdoers in this warning are those who disbelieved in their Lord.
rows.anchor: أخبرنا ابن وهب، قال: قال ابن زيد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explicitly glosses the wrongdoers for whom the fire is prepared as unbelievers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire’s surādiq is a wall of fire surrounding them like a tent enclosure; the word is illustrated by lines from Ruʾba and Salāma ibn Jandal.
rows.anchor: حائط من نار يطيف بهم كسرادق الفسطاط

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also interprets the enclosure as a wall of fire.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج، قال: قال ابن عباس، في قوله

rows.speaker: معمر
rows.claim: A report attributed to Maʿmar from an unnamed authority says the enclosure is smoke surrounding unbelievers, like the three-branched shade.
rows.anchor: عن معمر، عمن أخبره قال

rows.speaker: يعلى بن أمية
rows.claim: A Prophetic report from Yaʿlā ibn Umayya identifies the sea with Hell and takes the encircling enclosure as the sea in this world; the Prophet swore he would not enter it alive.
rows.anchor: عن صفوان بن يعلى، عن يعلى بن أمية

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: A Prophetic report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī says Hell’s enclosure has four walls, each as thick as a forty-year journey.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الهيثم، عن أبي سعيد الخدري، عن النبي

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: The Prophet says the fire’s enclosure consists of four walls, each as thick as a forty-year journey; its water is like oil sediment and burns the face when brought near.
rows.anchor: عن دراج، عن أبي الهيثم، عن أبي سعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Fire, the wrongdoers’ thirst prompts them to ask for water, but they are given molten-like water.
rows.anchor: ما رأينا في الدنيا شبيها للمهل أدنى من هذا الذهب والفضة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda relates that Ibn Masʿūd melted a gold-and-silver drinking vessel, then said this was the closest worldly likeness to maḥl.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قال: ذكر لنا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets maḥl as pus and black blood, like the sediment of oil.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes maḥl as black like oil or thick like its sediment.
rows.anchor: ثني معاوية، عن علي، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says Hell’s water is black, as are Hell, its trees, and its inhabitants.
rows.anchor: سمعت الضحاك، يقول في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās calls it thick water like oil sediment.
rows.anchor: عن أبيه، عن ابن عباس، قوله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says maḥl is something brought to its maximum heat.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير، قال: المهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These apparently different descriptions converge: molten lead, gold, or silver reaches extreme heat, and burning it to oil sediment also leaves it at maximum heat.
rows.anchor: فمتقاربات المعنى، وذلك أن كل ما أذيب

rows.speaker: المنتجع بن نبهان
rows.claim: Al-Muntajiʿ ibn Nabḥān describes maḥl as liquid heated to its limit, or a solid melted by fire until it reaches extreme heat, comparing it with molten residue from baking.
rows.anchor: فالمهل إذا هو كل مائع قد أوقد عليه حتى بلغ غاية حره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water they are given sears their faces.
rows.anchor: فإذا قرب منه شوى وجهه، ووقعت فروة رأسه

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: A Prophetic report on 14:17 says the drinker recoils; when brought near it sears his face and scalp, and when swallowed cuts his intestines.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أمامة، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، في قوله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr describes the sequence: the starving inhabitants eat from Zaqqum until facial skin is stripped, then thirst and receive scorching maḥl that burns the exposed flesh.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير، قال هارون: إذا جاع أهل النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The drink is evil, and the Fire is a terrible resting place; in Arabic, a place of irtifāq is where one leans or rests on an elbow.
rows.anchor: وساءت هذه النار التي أعتدناها لهؤلاء الظالمين مرتفقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s line uses مرتفقا for leaning on an elbow; Abū Dhuʾayb likewise describes spending the night leaning on his elbow.
rows.anchor: نام الخلي وبت الليل مرتفقا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets مرتفقا as a gathering place.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، {مرتفقا} [الكهف: 29] أي مجتمعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says he does not know irtifāq to mean gathering in Arabic; its derivation is from elbow or gentleness.
rows.anchor: ولست أعرف الارتفاق بمعنى الاجتماع في كلام العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden’s owner should have said that what God willed had happened when he entered and admired it; the conditional response, that it happened, is omitted but understood.
rows.anchor: وهلا إذ دخلت بستانك، فأعجبك ما رأيت منه، قلت ما شاء الله كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this parsing, ما is accusative as the object of شاء, and the answer to the conditional is understood though unspoken.
rows.anchor: كانت «ما» نصبا بوقوع فعل الله عليه، وهو شاء، وجاز طرح الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another Arabist parses ما as nominative with هو understood, yielding the sense it is what God willed.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض أهل العربية يقول «ما» من قوله: {ما شاء الله} [الأنعام: 128] في موضع رفع بإضمار هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لا قوة إلا بالله means that one has no ability to carry out the sought obedience except through God.
rows.anchor: لا قوة على ما نحاول من طاعته إلا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line إن ترن انا أقل منك is spoken by the poor believer to the garden’s wealthy owner; the believer is compared to Salmān, Ṣuhayb, and Khabbāb.
rows.anchor: عندنا، لأن عليه قراءة الأمصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When أنا is an inserted supporting pronoun, أقل is accusative; this is the reading adopted by the regional readers and al-Ṭabarī.
rows.anchor: عندنا، لأن عليه قراءة الأمصار، وإذا جعلته اسما رفعت أقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If أنا is instead treated as the subject, then أقل takes the nominative.
rows.anchor: وإذا جعلته اسما رفعت أقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A calamity destroyed the garden’s crops and fruit, which the owner once thought could never perish; he turned his hands over in grief at his lost investment.
rows.anchor: يقلب كفيه ظهرا لبطن، تلهفا وأسفا على ذهاب نفقته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains turning the hands as clapping them in regret.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، {فأصبح يقلب كفيه} [الكهف: 42] أي يصفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden is empty and collapsed over its supports; the owner wishes he had not associated anyone with God.
rows.anchor: وهي خالية على نباتها وبيوتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After his possessions disappear and he is left alone with his deeds, the unbeliever regrets having disbelieved or associated anything with God.
rows.anchor: إذا هلك وزالت عنه دنياه وانفرد بعمله، ود أنه لم يكن كفر بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly-life parable addresses arrogant people who asked that the believers devoted to God be expelled: worldly life is like rain-fed growth that soon dries and scatters.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء الذين يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي، إذا نحن جئناك الدنيا منهم مثلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plant becomes dry fragments scattered by winds; ذرو describes scattering, with several Arabic verb forms for blowing something away.
rows.anchor: فأصبح نبات الأرض يابسا متفتتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s line using يذرك illustrates the sense of casting or blowing someone off a mount.
rows.anchor: فيذرك من أخرى القطاة فتزلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can ruin gardens and worldly wealth; people should not boast or grow arrogant over wealth, since worldly life fades, while they should work for the enduring afterlife.
rows.anchor: ولكن ليعمل للباقي الذي لا يفنى، والدائم الذي لا يبيد ولا يتغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prior decree and appointed term prevent the people from being destroyed before their allotted time; lāzim is the verbal noun of lāzama, meaning something that would have adhered.
rows.anchor: يخترمه قبل بلوغه أجله {وأجل مسمى} [الأنعام: 2] يقول: ووقت مسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording places لكان لزاما before وأجل مسمى, but the sense is that without the prior word and an appointed term, destruction would have come immediately.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الكلام: ولولا كلمة سبقت من ربك وأجل مسمى لكان لزاما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the appointed term as the present worldly life.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، قوله: {ولولا كلمة سبقت من ربك لكان لزاما وأجل مسمى} [طه: 129] الأجل المسمى: الدنيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda treats the wording as fronted and delayed; the appointed term is the Hour, supported by the statement that the Hour is their promised time.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {ولولا كلمة سبقت من ربك لكان لزاما وأجل مسمى} [طه: 129] وهذه من مقاديم الكلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets لكان لزاما as death, while Ibn Zayd calls it killing.
rows.anchor: عن علي، عن ابن عباس، قوله: {لكان لزاما} [طه: 129] يقول: موتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should endure his people’s accusations that he is a sorcerer, madman, poet, and similar insults.
rows.anchor: فاصبر يا محمد على ما يقول هؤلاء المكذبون بآيات الله من قومك لك إنك ساحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سبح بحمد ربك means pray while praising your Lord; the construction makes God’s praise the object, as in the phrase I admire Zayd’s striking, meaning my striking Zayd.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: بحمدك ربك، كما تقول: أعجبني ضرب زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before sunrise means the dawn prayer, before sunset the afternoon prayer, and the night intervals refer to the evening prayer after part of the night has passed.
rows.anchor: وذلك صلاة الصبح {وقبل غروبها} [طه: 130] وهي العصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ānāʾ means the hours or periods of night, with singular inī; an unnamed line by al-Munkhil al-Saʿdī illustrates the word’s use for a night period.
rows.anchor: وهي ساعات الليل، واحدها: إني، على تقدير حمل
